clinicalPearls: SPG19 is a rare autosomal dominant, pure (uncomplicated) form of hereditary spastic paraplegia, defined by linkage to a locus on the long arm of chromosome 9 (9q33-q34) rather than by an identified gene.
Onset is typically in adult life, with insidiously progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness reflecting a length-dependent corticospinal tract axonopathy.
Core signs are a spastic gait, brisk lower-limb reflexes, extensor plantar responses and spasticity out of proportion to weakness.
Mild dorsal column sensory disturbance (reduced vibration sense at the toes) and urinary urgency may occur, in keeping with a pure HSP phenotype.
Cognition, cerebellar function, vision and the upper limbs are characteristically spared, distinguishing SPG19 from complicated subtypes.
Because no gene has been cloned, diagnosis rests on the phenotype, a dominant family history and exclusion of the common genes (SPAST/SPG4, ATL1/SPG3A, REEP1/SPG31).
Management is symptomatic: antispasticity measures, physiotherapy to preserve range of movement, and treatment of bladder overactivity.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG19 is a pure autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia originally mapped by linkage analysis to chromosome 9q33-q34 in a single kindred; to date no causative gene has been definitively identified within the interval, so the molecular mechanism remains inferred rather than proven. Like other forms of HSP it is understood to represent a distal, length-dependent axonopathy (dying-back degeneration) of the longest fibres of the corticospinal tracts and, to a lesser extent, the dorsal columns, producing the characteristic spastic paraparesis. The genes established for other dominant pure subtypes in the differential converge on membrane and organelle shaping, axonal transport and mitochondrial maintenance (for example spastin, atlastin-1 and REEP1), and the candidate gene for SPG19 is presumed to participate in similar neuronal housekeeping pathways that sustain the very long central motor axons most vulnerable in this disorder.
additionalDifferentials: SPG4 (SPAST/spastin) — the commonest autosomal dominant pure HSP and the first gene to exclude
SPG3A (ATL1/atlastin-1) — dominant pure HSP, typically earlier childhood onset
SPG31 (REEP1) and SPG6 (NIPA1) — other dominant pure HSP subtypes
Primary lateral sclerosis and other upper motor neurone disorders
Compressive or structural myelopathy (cervical spondylotic disease, cord tumour)
Dopa-responsive dystonia presenting with lower-limb stiffness
additionalInvestigations: Targeted panel or exome genetic testing for known HSP genes (SPAST, ATL1, REEP1 and others), since no SPG19 gene test exists
MRI of the whole spine to exclude compressive or structural myelopathy
MRI brain to exclude thin corpus callosum, white matter disease or other complicating features
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to exclude a peripheral neuropathy and screen for lower motor neurone involvement
Very-long-chain fatty acids, vitamin B12, copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude metabolic myeloneuropathy
HTLV serology and relevant CSF studies to exclude infective or inflammatory myelopathy
redFlags: Rapid progression, a sensory level or early sphincter loss suggesting a compressive or inflammatory myelopathy rather than HSP
Prominent bulbar, upper-limb or lower motor neurone features raising concern for motor neurone disease
Cognitive decline, ataxia, seizures or visual failure indicating a complicated syndrome and an alternative diagnosis
Marked asymmetry or acute onset, which is atypical for a slowly progressive inherited paraparesis
reference.prognosis: SPG19 is slowly progressive over years to decades with life expectancy generally preserved. Most affected people retain independent or aided walking for a prolonged period, although many eventually need walking aids as lower-limb spasticity and weakness accumulate.
pitfalls: Assuming a negative HSP gene panel excludes inherited disease — SPG19 has no clinical gene test and remains a linkage-defined, clinical diagnosis
Overlooking a treatable compressive myelopathy by attributing all spasticity to HSP without spinal imaging
Mislabelling adult-onset dominant paraparesis as multiple sclerosis when there are no relapses and no optic or brain lesions
Failing to take a detailed multigenerational family history, which is essential given the dominant inheritance
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical genetics reviews
Neurogenetics reference databases (gene and locus catalogues)
management: No gene-directed therapy exists; manage lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine, escalating to focal botulinum toxin for focal hypertonia
Physiotherapy, stretching and ankle-foot orthoses with walking aids to sustain gait and prevent contractures
Treat urinary urgency with antimuscarinic agents alongside urological review
Consider intrathecal baclofen for spasticity refractory to oral and focal measures
Surveillance of mobility, falls risk and contractures with occupational-therapy support
Genetic counselling and cascade testing for autosomal dominant inheritance
Re-evaluate the diagnosis if cerebellar, visual, cognitive or upper-limb signs emerge, as these argue against pure SPG19
